title: Balancing New DP1 Onboarding With DP2 IA Supervision
summary: A practical September-November plan for balancing new DP1 onboarding with DP2 IA supervision, feedback, standardization, and teacher workload.
body_markdown:
Balancing new DP1 onboarding with DP2 supervision is one of the hardest demands of the **IB teacher fall term** . DP1 students need explicit instruction in unfamiliar routines, while DP2 students need timely Internal Assessment guidance without receiving excessive assistance.


The most effective approach is to create two predictable systems: a concise DP1 induction programme that builds independence and a DP2 IA pipeline based on fixed milestones, short conferences, criterion-focused feedback, and protected standardization time. The September-November plan below shows how to manage both cohorts without allowing either to consume every planning period.


### Why the fall term becomes overloaded


DP1 and DP2 require different kinds of attention. DP1 students are learning command terms, assessment criteria, source use, academic integrity, independent study, and subject-specific expectations. When these foundations remain implicit, misunderstandings become repeated emails, incomplete work, and avoidable interventions.


DP2 pressure is more immediate. Students may be collecting evidence, refining research questions, completing analysis, or responding to permitted feedback. Because the sequence and feedback rules vary by subject, teachers must follow the **current subject guide** , school assessment calendar, and DP coordinator's instructions.


Attention should therefore be allocated by risk, not divided equally every week. Establish DP1 routines early, then move more protected time toward DP2 coursework as internal deadlines approach.


### Start with one coordinated assessment calendar


Identify every relevant DP2 milestone before planning the term. These may include proposal checks, data collection, oral components, draft submission, feedback, final submission, standardization, authentication, and upload preparation.


Schools normally set **internal deadlines** earlier than IB submission dates so marking, moderation, authentication, and administrative checks can be completed. Distinguish among three dates:


- **Student deadline:** work reaches the teacher
- **Department deadline:** marking and standardization are completed
- **Coordinator deadline:** authenticated files, marks, and supporting material are ready


Work backwards from the coordinator deadline and include contingency time for absences, inaccessible files, missing citations, technical problems, and academic-integrity reviews.


### A September-November operating plan


This model suits schools starting in August or September and preparing for a May examination session. Schools using another calendar can preserve the sequence while changing the months.


Period DP1 priority DP2 IA priority Protected teacher action


Early September Explain course structure, routines, command terms, and independent study Audit each student's IA stage and identify high-risk cases Build one tracker and confirm deadlines


Late September Diagnose prior knowledge and teach referencing through a short task Check question feasibility, evidence, or method progress Hold brief triage conferences


October Develop research, self-management, and criterion literacy Receive planned sections or drafts under subject rules Give criterion-focused feedback in batches


Early November Review routines through reflection and formative evidence Monitor revision, authenticity, and citations Standardize selected anchor samples


Late November Consolidate learning for the next teaching block Complete the next IA milestone or final checks Record decisions and escalate concerns


By October, induction should be embedded in subject learning rather than continuing as a separate presentation series.


### Build focused DP1 onboarding


DP1 students do not need every rule during their first week. They need the information required to make sound decisions now, followed by further guidance when it becomes relevant.


The first month should cover:


- Subject structure at **SL and HL** , where applicable
- Differences among formative work, school assessment, and IB assessment
- Command terms and criterion language
- Course resources, deadlines, policies, and support routes
- File organization, source use, and feedback records
- Academic integrity and permitted AI use
- How and when to request help


Use one low-stakes task to teach several routines. Students could answer a source-based question, cite the source, submit it correctly, examine the relevant criterion, and record one improvement target. This produces diagnostic evidence while rehearsing the complete workflow.


Introduce the IA's purpose early, but delay detailed instruction about design, methods, or criteria until students possess enough subject knowledge to apply it meaningfully.


### Manage DP2 IA supervision as a pipeline


A single deadline labelled "IA draft due" hides too much. Use a tracker showing each student's current stage, last checkpoint, main obstacle, next student action, next teacher action, conference date, feedback status, and authentication status.


Group students by need. Routine confirmation may require two minutes, while an unworkable method needs a focused conference. The[guided IA supervision framework](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/turning-ia-supervision-into-a-guided-learning-journey) provides a milestone model that departments can adapt.


### Use short, structured conferences


A **5-10 minute conference** can address four questions: What has been completed? What evidence demonstrates progress? What prevents the next step? What will the student complete, and by when?


Record the agreed action. Students should leave responsible for the next intellectual decision, without receiving teacher-generated wording or analysis.


### Batch criterion-focused feedback


Where subject rules permit, review one common element across the cohort, such as question focus, evidence, evaluation, or citation practice. A concise criterion-linked comment bank reduces repeated typing, but the diagnosis must remain specific to the student's work. RevisionDojo's guide to[delivering better IA feedback efficiently](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-ib-teachers-can-deliver-better-ia-feedback-in-less-time) explains this approach.


### Keep feedback within IB boundaries


Permitted support differs across subjects and components. Confirm what may be discussed before drafting, whether a draft can receive feedback, the permitted extent of that feedback, what must remain the student's decision, and how authenticity is confirmed.


Feedback should identify weaknesses and redirect students to criteria, evidence, or reasoning. It should not rewrite passages, provide conclusions, correct every sentence, or create submission-ready material.


The IB does not impose a blanket ban on AI tools, but generated material is not automatically the student's own work. Schools should specify permitted uses, require transparency where relevant, and teach students to verify outputs.


### Protect standardization and authenticity


Internal assessment is marked by teachers and may be moderated by the IB, making departmental standardization essential. Before marking the entire cohort, select anchor samples at different levels, mark them independently, compare criterion-level judgments, and record agreed interpretations. RevisionDojo's guide to[IA consistency and departmental standardization](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/using-revisiondojo-to-standardize-internal-assessments-across-departments) offers a practical structure.


Establish authenticity throughout the process. Retain proposals, notes, sources, draft versions, conference records, and evidence showing how thinking developed. Escalate serious concerns through the school's academic-integrity procedure.


### Protect teacher workload deliberately


Reserve separate calendar blocks for DP1 planning, DP2 feedback, conferences, and standardization. Practical boundaries include accepting work through one channel, using fixed conference windows, marking manageable batches, maintaining one tracker, and escalating missed milestones early.


RevisionDojo's[teacher and department guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-for-ib-teachers-departments) explains how assignments, analytics, the Questionbank, and coursework feedback can support repeated tasks. Automated feedback should remain diagnostic because teachers retain responsibility for applying official criteria, observing feedback restrictions, protecting data, and making assessment decisions.


### Common mistakes to avoid


- Completing DP1 induction in one presentation instead of revisiting expectations through subject tasks
- Giving every DP2 student equal conference time instead of triaging support fairly
- Treating internal deadlines as continuously negotiable
- Writing exhaustive feedback that creates dependence or exceeds permitted assistance
- Delaying standardization until most marking is finished


### Conclusion


Balancing DP1 onboarding with DP2 IA supervision requires a concise induction sequence and a milestone-based IA pipeline. Clear deadlines, targeted conferences, criterion-focused feedback, early standardization, and process evidence protect assessment quality and teacher capacity.


RevisionDojo can support this structure through its[IB resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib) , Questionbank, Study Notes, class tools, and coursework feedback. Questionbank can support DP1 diagnostic practice, while Coursework Review can provide secondary diagnostic support for DP2. Teacher judgment and the current IB guide remain the final authority.
